transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Flights are resuming across the United States following an hours-long ground stop last night.
Problems with radar and communication systems prompted the FAA to halt departures at airports across the country.
Passengers on a plane traveling from Detroit to Fort Lauderdale were in the air when the pilot announced
there was a problem.
Ground stop throughout the U.S., there's a due to frequency issue.
So that's all we have right now.
Everything's on time.
We're still heading to Fort Lauderdale.
Plan on landing there in about 50 minutes.
Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen says passengers were never in danger.
There was never any lives at risk.
There was no flights at risk.
FAA was able to handle it.
We did it out of an abundant of caution.
But I do understand the Internet traffic and where all these conspiracies start running towards.
FlightAware lists more than 3,300 cancellations and about 900 delays for flights within, into or out of the U.S. today.
Microsoft says it's seeing broad recovery and stability after a global outage of Outlook email and other applications this week.
NPR's Andrea Shue reports the disruption was felt far and wide and in different ways.
No doubt the widespread outage caused real mayhem for many individuals and workplaces.
Hospitals in the U.K. found themselves dealing with paper records as their systems became unusable.
Congressional staffers scrambled to keep key conversations going.
But for some others, it was a welcome respite.
Caroline Berdzik says she was fortunate.
The employment attorney did not have any filing deadlines to meet that day.
Without the constant digging of emails, she had an extremely productive day, focusing on motions and briefs.
Efficiency is a good thing, but I think we need to press pause from time to time and reflect.
For her at least, the outage was both inconvenient and glorious.
Andrea Shue, NPR News.
Republican Representative Lauren Boebert has lost her bid for re-election in a conservative stronghold.
Paulo Shalsita from Colorado Public Radio has more.
Boebert is among the many Republican incumbents who lost their seats to Democratic challengers.
Her tenure in Congress has been marked by numerous controversies, earning a statewide and national reputation as a political firebrand.
When she spoke to reporters on Monday, she said she doesn't blame any one particular person for the massive losses that Republicans experience in the midterms.
Republicans need to listen to voters, not political pundits and consultants.
I wish that more of us could have been listened to by our own leadership here at times.
Democrat Eileen Laubaucker, a retired Navy Rear Admiral, will take office in January.
For NPR News, I'm Paulo Shalsita in Denver.
This is NPR News in Washington.
A federal rule requiring stores that accept SNAP benefits to stock more fresh and perishable foods has been delayed after going into effect earlier this month.
As Macy Byers reports, small grocers and convenience stores said it would be hard to comply.
New York City Mayor Zoran Mamdani, in partnership with the National Association of Convenience Stores, announced they had brokered a deal with President Trump for a 90-day delay.
Many small and rural grocery stores have opposed the new requirements, saying they may not have the resources to comply.
Carly Jonas with the Nebraska-based Center for Rural Affairs says that could lead stores to drop their SNAP retailer status.
They want to be able to have SNAP and people be able to access it because it does help support their business and feed people in their community.
And it's just conflicting because they also are operating on such in-profit margins that they don't want to risk getting in trouble.
Supporters of the delay say it will give retailers more time to adjust.
For NPR News, I'm Macy Byers in Lincoln, Nebraska.
The Trump administration will allow states to delay cutting off Medicaid coverage for people who fail to meet new work requirements.
States can postpone those coverage losses until July 1st, rather than starting in January.
The requirements apply to certain adults who must work, volunteer, or participate in other qualifying activities unless exempt.
States choosing the delay must still check whether people meet the rules.
Federal officials say the extra time will help states improve their systems and avoid mistakes that could disrupt coverage.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: FAA halts and then resumes flights nationwide after radar and communication system problems
Microsoft Outlook global outage disrupts hospitals and offices, while some workers welcome the break
Republican Representative Lauren Boebert loses reelection bid in her Colorado conservative district
Federal rule requiring SNAP stores to stock fresh foods delayed after small grocers protest compliance costs
Trump administration lets states delay Medicaid coverage cuts for failing new work requirements until July
